definition: The delay between sending a request and getting the first response back.
example: Pressing a game button and seeing your character jump 40ms later.
whyItMatters: Low latency makes multiplayer games and video calls feel instant.

definition: A clear step-by-step recipe a computer follows to solve a problem.
example: Binary search finds a word in a dictionary by splitting it in half each step.
whyItMatters: Smart algorithms turn hours of searching into milliseconds.

definition: A fast temporary storage spot that keeps copies of data you recently used.
example: Your browser saves a site's logo so it loads instantly on your next visit.
whyItMatters: Caching saves bandwidth and makes apps feel snappy.

definition: Scrambling a message with a secret key so only authorized people can read it.
example: Turning 'HELLO' into 'KHOOR' by shifting each letter 3 spots.
whyItMatters: Encryption keeps your messages, passwords, and Wi-Fi private.

definition: The maximum amount of data that can travel over a connection each second.
example: A 100 Mbps connection can download a large game much faster than 10 Mbps.
whyItMatters: High bandwidth lets multiple people stream video at the same time.

definition: The smallest unit of computer data, holding either a 0 or a 1.
example: A light switch being either OFF (0) or ON (1).
whyItMatters: Every photo, song, and video game is built from billions of bits.

definition: A group of 8 bits, enough to store one simple letter or small number.
example: The word 'CAT' takes 3 bytes in plain ASCII text.
whyItMatters: File sizes like megabytes and gigabytes are counted in bytes.

definition: A base-2 counting system using only the digits 0 and 1.
example: In binary, the number 5 is written as 101 (4 + 0 + 1).
whyItMatters: Computer chips use electrical voltages that represent 0s and 1s.

definition: A base-16 number system using 0–9 and A–F to write binary compactly.
example: Bright red in web colors is #FF0000.
whyItMatters: Programmers use hex for colors, memory addresses, and MAC addresses.

definition: The Central Processing Unit—the main brain inside a computer that runs instructions.
example: A modern CPU performs billions of math and logic steps every second.
whyItMatters: Determines how fast your computer or phone thinks.

definition: A Graphics Processing Unit built to run thousands of simple math tasks in parallel.
example: Drawing millions of 3D pixels 60 times a second in a game.
whyItMatters: Also powers modern AI training and video editing.

definition: Random Access Memory—fast short-term memory holding apps currently open.
example: Having 16 GB of RAM lets you keep many browser tabs and games open smoothly.
whyItMatters: RAM clears when power turns off, unlike an SSD.

definition: A Solid-State Drive that stores files permanently on flash chips with no moving parts.
example: Saving your photos and games so they are still there after rebooting.
whyItMatters: Much faster and tougher than old spinning hard drives.

definition: The master software that manages hardware, files, and apps on a device.
example: Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android.
whyItMatters: Without an OS, apps couldn't talk to the screen, keyboard, or internet.

definition: The core heart of an operating system that directly controls CPU, memory, and devices.
example: The Linux kernel runs everything from Android phones to space rockets.
whyItMatters: Keeps programs from crashing into each other's memory.

definition: A program that translates human-readable source code into fast machine code.
example: Turning C++ or Rust code into a runnable Windows app.
whyItMatters: Lets programmers write readable code that still runs at full speed.

definition: A program that reads and runs source code line by line on the fly.
example: Python and JavaScript engines execute code directly.
whyItMatters: Makes testing and experimenting with code super fast.

definition: Application Programming Interface—a clean menu of rules letting two programs talk.
example: A weather app asking a weather server for today's forecast JSON.
whyItMatters: Allows apps to share maps, payments, and live feeds safely.

definition: JavaScript Object Notation—a lightweight text format for storing and sending structured data.
example: {"name": "Yuval", "score": 100}
whyItMatters: Almost every web API sends data in JSON.

definition: HyperText Markup Language—the skeleton that defines headings, links, and paragraphs on web pages.
example:
Hello!

creates a main heading.
whyItMatters: Every website you visit starts as HTML.

definition: Cascading Style Sheets—the language that controls colors, fonts, borders, and layout on the web.
example: color: #111111; border-radius: 20px;
whyItMatters: Turns plain HTML text into colorful, mobile-friendly designs.

definition: Document Object Model—the live tree of elements a browser builds from HTML.
example: JavaScript updates the DOM when you click a tab or filter chip.
whyItMatters: Makes web pages interactive without reloading the whole page.

definition: Hypertext Transfer Protocol—the rulebook browsers and servers use to request web pages.
example: Your browser sends GET / to ask a server for the homepage.
whyItMatters: It is the foundation of the World Wide Web.

definition: Encrypted HTTP using TLS so nobody in between can spy on or tamper with your traffic.
example: The padlock icon in your browser bar on banking or login sites.
whyItMatters: Protects passwords and private messages on public Wi-Fi.

definition: Domain Name System—the internet's phonebook translating names into numeric IP addresses.
example: Turning yuval.melameds.net into the server's IP address.
whyItMatters: Lets humans use memorable names instead of strings of numbers.

definition: A unique numeric label assigned to every device connected to a network.
example: 192.168.1.1 on a home router or 2001:db8::1 in IPv6.
whyItMatters: Routers use IP addresses to deliver packets to the right device.

definition: A small chunk of data sent across a network with a sender and destination label.
example: A video stream broken into thousands of tiny packets.
whyItMatters: Splitting data into packets lets millions of users share the same cables.

definition: A networking device that forwards data packets along the best path toward their destination.
example: Your home Wi-Fi box connecting phones and laptops to the internet.
whyItMatters: Directs global internet traffic in milliseconds.

definition: A security guard that inspects network traffic and blocks unauthorized connections.
example: Allowing web traffic on port 443 while blocking unknown scanners.
whyItMatters: Keeps private computers and servers safe from attacks.

definition: Virtual Private Network—an encrypted tunnel between your device and another network.
example: Connecting safely to a school or office network from home.
whyItMatters: Hides traffic from snoops on untrusted public networks.

definition: A computer or program that waits for requests and sends back data or web pages.
example: Vercel and Neon servers powering your Daily Dose page.
whyItMatters: Powers websites, multiplayer games, and cloud backups.

definition: Renting computing power, storage, and databases over the internet instead of owning hardware.
example: Hosting an app on Vercel instead of running a PC in your closet 24/7.
whyItMatters: Lets small teams launch global apps in minutes.

definition: A cloud model where your code runs on demand without you managing any servers.
example: A function waking up for 50ms to handle a login request.
whyItMatters: Scales automatically and costs $0 when nobody is visiting.

definition: An organized system for storing, searching, and updating large amounts of data.
example: Postgres storing daily history events and news headlines.
whyItMatters: Almost every app needs a database to remember state.

definition: Structured Query Language—the standard language for asking questions to relational databases.
example: SELECT title FROM feed_items LIMIT 10;
whyItMatters: Has powered banks, hospitals, and apps for over 50 years.

definition: A sorted lookup structure that lets a database find rows fast without scanning everything.
example: Like the alphabetical index at the back of an encyclopedia.
whyItMatters: Turns a 5-second search into a 2-millisecond query.

definition: A unique ID column that identifies every single row in a database table.
example: User ID #42 or a unique SHA-256 item hash.
whyItMatters: Prevents duplicate records and links tables cleanly.

definition: A tiny piece of data a website stores in your browser to remember you.
example: Keeping you logged in after you type the password once.
whyItMatters: HttpOnly signed cookies keep web sessions secure.

definition: A browser storage space where websites can save small settings on your device.
example: Saving your 'What is your take?' answer and mission checklist.
whyItMatters: Works offline and remembers preferences without a server round-trip.

definition: A one-way math function turning any data into a fixed-length digital fingerprint.
example: SHA-256 turning 'hello' into a 64-character hex string.
whyItMatters: Verifies file downloads and secures passwords.

definition: Requiring two proofs of identity—something you know (password) and something you have (phone code).
example: Entering your password plus a 6-digit code from an app.
whyItMatters: Stops hackers even if they guess or steal your password.

definition: Software whose source code is public so anyone can inspect, learn from, and improve it.
example: Linux, Python, React, and PostgreSQL.
whyItMatters: Powers most of the modern internet through shared collaboration.

definition: A version control system that tracks every change made to code over time.
example: Committing a new feature on a branch and rolling back if something breaks.
whyItMatters: Lets developers collaborate safely without overwriting each other.

definition: A proposal to merge code changes from a feature branch into the main project after review.
example: Opening a PR on GitHub for teammates to inspect your diff.
whyItMatters: Catches bugs before they reach live users.

definition: Continuous Integration & Continuous Deployment—automated testing and releasing on every code push.
example: Running tests automatically and deploying to Vercel when they pass.
whyItMatters: Makes shipping updates fast and reliable.

definition: An automated check that tests one small function in isolation.
example: Verifying sanitizeHttpUrl rejects 'javascript:alert(1)'.
whyItMatters: Catches regressions in seconds before deployment.

definition: An unintended mistake in code that causes wrong behavior or a crash.
example: An off-by-one loop missing the last item in a list.
whyItMatters: Testing and clear logs help squash bugs quickly.

definition: The detective work of finding and fixing the root cause of a bug.
example: Checking server logs to see why an RSS feed returned 0 items.
whyItMatters: Every great programmer spends lots of time debugging cleanly.

definition: A report listing the exact chain of function calls running when an error happened.
example: Showing file name and line number where a crash occurred.
whyItMatters: Points developers straight to the broken line of code.

definition: When a function solves a big problem by calling itself on smaller pieces.
example: Searching every folder inside folders on your computer.
whyItMatters: Makes tree and maze algorithms clean and concise.

definition: An ordered collection of items stored under a single variable name, indexed from 0.
example: ['Events', 'Births', 'Deaths'] where index 0 is 'Events'.
whyItMatters: One of the most basic building blocks in all code.

definition: A data structure storing key-value pairs for near-instant lookups.
example: Looking up a scientist by date key '11-22' directly.
whyItMatters: Powers dictionaries, caches, and fast deduplication.

definition: A First-In, First-Out (FIFO) list where the earliest item added is handled first.
example: Jobs waiting in line for a printer.
whyItMatters: Keeps background tasks fair and orderly.

definition: A Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) list like a stack of plates.
example: Your browser's Back button and Undo (Ctrl+Z).
whyItMatters: Tracks function calls and undo history.

definition: Finding an item in a sorted list by repeatedly cutting the search space in half.
example: Guessing a number 1–100 in at most 7 tries by always guessing the middle.
whyItMatters: Finds 1 item out of a billion in ~30 steps.

definition: A shorthand describing how an algorithm's runtime grows as input size grows.
example: O(1) is instant; O(n) grows with list size; O(log n) halves each step.
whyItMatters: Helps engineers avoid code that slows down on big data.

definition: Shrinking files by removing repeating or less-noticeable patterns.
example: ZIP files, PNG images, and MP3 audio.
whyItMatters: Saves storage space and speeds up downloads.

definition: The smallest single colored dot on a digital screen or image.
example: A 1920×1080 screen has over 2 million pixels.
whyItMatters: More pixels per inch means sharper text and photos.

definition: Scalable Vector Graphics—images drawn from math shapes instead of pixel grids.
example: Our Daily Dose icons and grass strip stay sharp at any zoom.
whyItMatters: Tiny file sizes and never look blurry on Retina screens.

definition: How many still pictures a screen or game draws each second.
example: 60 FPS means a fresh frame every 16.7 milliseconds.
whyItMatters: Higher FPS makes motion look silky smooth.

definition: Teaching computers to spot patterns from examples rather than explicit if/else rules.
example: Learning to recognize handwritten digits from thousands of photos.
whyItMatters: Powers voice assistants, translation, and medical imaging.

definition: An AI system inspired by connected brain neurons that adjusts weights during training.
example: Recognizing whether a photo shows a cat or a dog.
whyItMatters: Forms the foundation of modern speech and language AI.

definition: A small chunk of text (a word or part of a word) that a language model reads and predicts.
example: 'unbelievable' might split into ['un', 'believ', 'able'].
whyItMatters: AI models process and measure speed in tokens per second.

definition: A trick where untrusted text tries to hijack an AI assistant's instructions.
example: Hiding fake instructions inside a web page an AI is summarizing.
whyItMatters: AI systems must treat web text strictly as data, never commands.

definition: A lightweight packaged box holding an app and everything it needs to run anywhere.
example: Shipping the exact same app environment from laptop to cloud.
whyItMatters: Eliminates 'it worked on my machine' problems.

definition: A full simulated computer running inside another physical computer.
example: Running Linux inside a window on a Windows PC.
whyItMatters: Lets cloud providers safely share big servers across customers.

definition: A scheduled task that runs automatically at set times or intervals.
example: Refreshing Today in History every morning at 07:00.
whyItMatters: Automates backups, reports, and daily updates.

definition: An automated HTTP message sent when an event happens in another system.
example: GitHub notifying Vercel to rebuild right after a git push.
whyItMatters: Connects apps in real time without constant polling.

definition: Capping how many requests a user can send in a time window.
example: Locking login after 5 wrong passwords in 15 minutes.
whyItMatters: Stops brute-force attacks and protects servers from overload.

definition: A traffic director that spreads incoming users evenly across multiple servers.
example: Sending half of visitors to Server A and half to Server B.
whyItMatters: Keeps popular websites fast and online if one server fails.

definition: Content Delivery Network—servers around the world storing copies of files near users.
example: Serving images from a nearby edge node instead of halfway around Earth.
whyItMatters: Makes websites load dramatically faster worldwide.

definition: A temporary memory of recent domain-to-IP lookups on your device or router.
example: Remembering google.com's IP so pages open faster.
whyItMatters: Cuts down millions of repeat lookups every second.

definition: A universal standard assigning a unique number to every letter, symbol, and emoji in every language.
example: English 'A', Hebrew 'א', and chess '♔' all have Unicode code points.
whyItMatters: Lets one web page mix English, Hebrew, math, and chess symbols cleanly.

definition: The most popular way to encode Unicode characters into bytes on the web.
example: English letters take 1 byte; Hebrew letters take 2 bytes; emojis take 4.
whyItMatters: Used by over 98% of websites worldwide.

definition: Regular Expression—a compact pattern language for matching and cleaning text.
example: Checking if a string looks like YYYY-MM-DD.
whyItMatters: Used everywhere for search, validation, and data parsing.
